extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic drama: principles of plot, recognition, character, diction, and the mechanics of language as set out in a classical poetics. Emphasises unity, naturalness of incidents, and appropriate use of language and choral/performative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrational elements or keep them outside the tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the irrational cannot be excluded, it should be outside the scope of the tragedy. Such is the irrational element in the Oedipus of Sophocles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational or supernatural elements weaken the art of tragedy when they are integral to the plot; if they must appear, they should be external to the dramatic action so the plot remains intelligible and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of persons above the common level
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of persons who are above the common level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the example of good portrait-painters: reproduce distinctive form true to life but made more beautiful — present elevated characters rather than common folk to achieve tragic greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the character-type while ennobling it
rubrics_metrics.description: In representing men who are irascible or indolent, or have other defects of character, the poet should preserve the type and yet ennoble it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the recognizable traits of a character but idealise or heighten them so that flaws are expressive rather than merely realistic; examples include Achilles as portrayed by Agathon and Homer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory appeals cautiously (concomitants of poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should not neglect those appeals to the senses, which, though not among the essentials, are the concomitants of poetry; for here too there is much room for error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sensory detail to enhance poetry, but take care—overuse or clumsy sensory appeals can harm the piece; the treatment of such elements requires skill (further discussed elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by signs/tokens (least artistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by signs: congenital tokens or acquired bodily marks or external tokens (scars, necklaces, the ark). The use of tokens for the express purpose of proof is a less artistic mode of recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens can be used skilfully (e.g., Odysseus' scar) but are inherently less artful than recognitions arising from the plot itself; avoid depending on arbitrary tokens as a primary recognition device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by a turn of incident (better)
rubrics_metrics.description: A better kind is that which comes about by a turn of incident, as in the Bath Scene in the Odyssey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create recognitions that naturally emerge from events' developments — incident-driven discoveries are more artistic and satisfying than token-based proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition invented at will by the poet (unartistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will by the poet, and on that account wanting in art—for example, a character revealing himself by speech because the poet wants him to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary authorial devices (e.g., making a character speak a revelation the plot does not require); such contrivances are nearly allied to the fault of using tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by memory (sight or sound triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition depending on memory when the sight of some object or hearing something awakens a feeling (e.g., seeing a picture, hearing a minstrel play the lyre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use memory-triggered recognitions where sensory stimuli naturally recall the past for a character — these can be effective but should feel grounded in the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by process of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by process of reasoning (e.g., 'Some one resembling me has come: no one resembles me but Orestes: therefore Orestes has come').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow characters to infer identities logically from circumstances; reasoning-based recognitions are more artistic than token-based ones and can feel natural if plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite recognition involving false inference (defective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite recognitions involving false inference (the expectation that another will recognise something he has not seen) produce recognition by inducing expectation rather than truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using false inferences as the basis for recognition — they rely on manipulation of characters' and audience's expectations and are less artful than natural incident-based discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best recognition arises from incidents themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all recognitions, the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves, where the startling discovery is made by natural means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for recognitions that flow inevitably from the plot's events (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia) because they dispense with artificial aids and are the most artistically satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize the scene vividly during composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes; seeing everything with the utmost vividness, as if he were a spectator of the action, he will discover what is in keeping with it, and be most unlikely to overlook inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work from a vivid mental staging of each scene to catch situational details and avoid errors that would offend an audience or break credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work out appropriate gestures and natural expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should work out his play, to the best of his power, with appropriate gestures; those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy with the characters they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design gestures and physical expression that flow from the characters' emotions; naturalistic, sympathetic acting details lend life-like reality to the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan: sketch general outline then fill in episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poet takes the story ready-made or constructs it, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a clear overall structure (main situation and turning point) and only then add episodes; this preserves unity and prevents extraneous digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be relevant to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: After the general plan, it remains to fill in the episodes. We must see that they are relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only episodes that serve the central plot or character development; irrelevant episodes dilute the tragic effect and are more suitable to epic length forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy structure: Complication and Unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts,—Complication and Unravelling or Dénouement. Complication: from beginning to the turning-point to good or bad fortune. Unravelling: from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the plot with a clear division: build to a decisive reversal/turning point, then resolve consequences through to the end — maintain causal unity between the parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy & use of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of Tragedy: the Complex (depending entirely on Reversal of the Situation and Recognition), the Pathetic (motive is passion), the Ethical (motives are ethical), and the Simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which type you aim for and include the relevant elements; strive to combine as many poetic elements as possible (reversal, recognition, pathos, ethical motive) for richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epic multiplicity of plots in tragedy; preserve unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should not make an Epic structure into a Tragedy—by an Epic structure I mean one with a multiplicity of plots... In the drama the result is far from answering to the poet’s expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single, unified plot appropriate to dramatic length; do not attempt to dramatize an entire epic tale with many subplots — focus yields stronger tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must be an integral actor in the drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and share in the action, in the manner not of Euripides but of Sophocles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral songs to participate in, comment on, or advance the action rather than as unrelated interludes or mere spectacle; integrate the chorus into the play's subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought: speech must effect proof, emotion, and suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought is included every effect which has to be produced by speech, the subdivisions being—proof and refutation; the excitation of the feelings, such as pity, fear, anger, and the like; the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft speeches to achieve rhetorical functions: establish arguments, refute, and arouse or modulate emotions; speeches should do their work through persuasive and evocative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat dramatic incidents like speeches when aiming at effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic incidents must be treated from the same points of view as the dramatic speeches, when the object is to evoke the sense of pity, fear, importance, or probability. The only difference is that the incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents so they naturally produce the intended emotional and moral effects (pity, fear, etc.) without relying on expository dialogue — show rather than tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of utterance (diction) and delivery awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch treats the Modes of Utterance (what is a command, a prayer, a statement, a threat, a question, an answer). This province belongs to the art of Delivery and to the masters of that science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of verbal modes and their intended performative force; while fine distinctions belong to delivery, poets should know what speech-types they intend and how those will be realized by performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to language mechanics for diction and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Language includes: Letter, Syllable, Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion or Case, Sentence or Phrase. Definitions of vowel, semi-vowel, mute, syllable, connecting word, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the basic elements of sound and word-formation (letters, syllables, connecting words) because they affect metre, rhythm, and diction; choices at the phonetic/morphological level influence poetic effect.
